title: What are the DDD tactical building blocks and how do they map to Java/Spring code — Entity, Value Object, Aggregate, Repository, Domain Service, Application Service — and what are the strategic DDD concepts: Bounded Context, Ubiquitous Language, Context Mapping, and Domain Events?
shortTitle: DDD tactical building blocks and strategic concepts

s1_definition.profdef: Domain-Driven Design has tactical building blocks for modeling inside a bounded context and strategic concepts for organizing across contexts. The tactical blocks are: an Entity, which has a unique identity and a mutable lifecycle, such as an `Account` with an account id; a Value Object, which has no identity, is immutable, and is compared by value, such as `Money`, modeled in Java as a `record`; an Aggregate, which is a cluster of entities and value objects treated as one consistency unit and accessed only through its Aggregate Root; a Repository, which abstracts persistence for an aggregate, such as `AccountRepository`; a Domain Service, which holds stateless domain logic that does not belong to a single entity; and an Application Service, which orchestrates a use case, manages the transaction, and calls domain services and repositories, mapping to the Spring `@Service` layer. The strategic concepts are Bounded Context, Ubiquitous Language, Context Mapping, and Domain Events.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, an Entity is like Rajesh's account: it has a unique number and its balance changes over time, so identity matters. A Value Object is like an amount of money, say 50,000 rupees: one 50,000-rupee note is interchangeable with any other, there is no identity, only value. An Aggregate is like a passbook treated as one unit: you only make changes through the front cover (the root), never by scribbling on random pages. A Repository is the filing clerk who fetches and stores a whole passbook. A Domain Service is the interest calculator that works across accounts and belongs to no single account. An Application Service is the bank officer who runs the whole "transfer money" procedure: opens the transaction, asks the clerk for the passbooks, applies the rules, and closes the transaction.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Domain-Driven Design has tactical building blocks for modeling inside a bounded context and strategic concepts for organizing across contexts. The tactical blocks are: an Entity, which has a unique identity and a mutable lifecycle, such as an `Account` with an account id; a Value Object, which has no identity, is immutable, and is compared by value, such as `Money`, modeled in Java as a `record`; an Aggregate, which is a cluster of entities and value objects treated as one consistency unit and accessed only through its Aggregate Root; a Repository, which abstracts persistence for an aggregate, such as `AccountRepository`; a Domain Service, which holds stateless domain logic that does not belong to a single entity; and an Application Service, which orchestrates a use case, manages the transaction, and calls domain services and repositories, mapping to the Spring `@Service` layer. The strategic concepts are Bounded Context, Ubiquitous Language, Context Mapping, and Domain Events.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, an Entity is like Rajesh's account: it has a unique number and its balance changes over time, so identity matters. A Value Object is like an amount of money, say 50,000 rupees: one 50,000-rupee note is interchangeable with any other, there is no identity, only value. An Aggregate is like a passbook treated as one unit: you only make changes through the front cover (the root), never by scribbling on random pages. A Repository is the filing clerk who fetches and stores a whole passbook. A Domain Service is the interest calculator that works across accounts and belongs to no single account. An Application Service is the bank officer who runs the whole "transfer money" procedure: opens the transaction, asks the clerk for the passbooks, applies the rules, and closes the transaction.

**One line to remember:** Entity has identity, Value Object is immutable value, Aggregate is one consistency unit via its root, Repository persists aggregates, Domain Service holds cross-entity logic, Application Service orchestrates use cases, and strategically Bounded Context, Ubiquitous Language, Context Mapping, and Domain Events organize everything.

sections.s2_technical:
An Entity has identity and a lifecycle. Two accounts with the same balance are still different accounts because they have different ids, so equality is by id, not by field values. In Java an `Account` entity has an `accountId`, mutable state like `balance`, and behavior like `debit` and `credit` that protect invariants. In Spring you annotate it `@Entity` with `@Id`.

A Value Object has no identity, is immutable, and is equal by value. `Money` holding an amount and a currency is a perfect example: 50,000 rupees equals any other 50,000 rupees, and you never mutate it, you create a new one. Java `record` is the ideal mapping because records are immutable and give value-based equality for free, for example `new Money(new BigDecimal("50000"), "INR")`. Using value objects removes a whole class of bugs where people pass raw `BigDecimal` and lose the currency.

An Aggregate is a cluster of entities and value objects that must stay consistent together, accessed only through its Aggregate Root. The root is the only entry point and enforces invariants, so you call `account.debit(money)` rather than reaching inside. A Repository abstracts persistence for one aggregate: `AccountRepository.findById(id)` loads the whole aggregate and `save(account)` stores it. In Spring Data this is `interface AccountRepository extends JpaRepository<Account, String>`. There is one repository per aggregate root, never per random table.

A Domain Service holds stateless domain logic that does not naturally belong to a single entity. Calculating interest across a product catalog or pricing a trade is domain logic but not the responsibility of one account, so it lives in a domain service. An Application Service sits one layer above: it orchestrates a use case, starts and commits the transaction, and coordinates repositories and domain services. In Spring this is the `@Service` annotated with `@Transactional` that implements "transfer money": it loads both aggregates, invokes their behavior, saves them, and publishes a domain event. The key rule is that application services contain no business rules; the rules live in entities and domain services.

Strategically, a Bounded Context is the boundary within which one model and one Ubiquitous Language are consistent, where the team uses the exact same words in code, docs, and conversation. Context Mapping describes how contexts relate, such as a shared kernel, a customer-supplier relationship, or an anti-corruption layer that translates another context's model at the border. Domain Events are records of something meaningful that happened, published to decouple contexts, so the Deposits context emits `FundsDebited` and the Lending context reacts without sharing a model. The senior-level nuance is that the tactical blocks keep a single service's model clean and the strategic concepts keep many services from collapsing into a tangled shared model.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India we are modeling the Deposits context cleanly. Problem 1 — money was passed around as a raw `BigDecimal`, and a bug once added rupees to dollars. This is exactly what a `Money` Value Object prevents: immutable, currency-aware, equal by value. Problem 2 — code reached inside the account to change the balance directly, breaking the "never negative" rule. This is exactly what an Aggregate Root fixes: all changes go through `account.debit(money)`. Problem 3 — the "transfer money" use case mixed transaction handling with business rules in one tangled method. This is exactly the split between an Application Service that orchestrates and an Entity plus Domain Service that hold the rules.

The mini-project models a `Money` value object (a record), an `Account` entity and aggregate root with `debit` and `credit`, an `AccountRepository` abstraction, a `TransferDomainService` holding the cross-account rule, an `TransferApplicationService` that orchestrates the use case and publishes a `FundsTransferredEvent`. A runnable demo transfers 50,000 from Rajesh to Priya and prints the published domain event.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, 1,000,000 INR), Priya (CUR3001, 250,000 INR), and a transfer of 50,000 INR.

Step 1: The amount 50,000 is wrapped in a `Money` value object with currency INR. It is immutable, so any arithmetic produces a new `Money`, and it refuses to mix currencies. The raw-`BigDecimal` bug is impossible here.

Step 2: The Application Service starts the use case. It asks the Repository to load both `Account` aggregates by their id. Identity, not balance, is what distinguishes the accounts.

Step 3: The Application Service delegates the business rule to the Domain Service, which calls `from.debit(money)` and `to.credit(money)`. Each change goes through the aggregate root, which enforces the never-negative invariant. Rajesh drops to 950,000 and Priya rises to 300,000.

Step 4: The Application Service saves both aggregates through the Repository, which in Spring would commit the transaction it owns. No business rule lives in the Application Service; it only orchestrates.

Step 5: The Application Service publishes a `FundsTransferredEvent` domain event carrying the from id, to id, and `Money`. Other bounded contexts, such as Notifications or Lending, can react to this event without sharing the Deposits model, which is the strategic decoupling DDD aims for.

```text
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:30 INFO === DDD transfer: Value Object + Entity + Repo + Domain + App Service ===

Oct 24, 2026 11:53:30 INFO CUR3001 credited, balance=300000
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:30 INFO Published domain event: FundsTransferredEvent[fromId=SAV2001, toId=CUR3001, amount=Money[amount=50000, currency=INR]]
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:30 INFO Rajesh balance: 950000
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:30 INFO Priya balance: 300000
Oct 24, 2026 11:53:30 INFO Domain event produced: FundsTransferredEvent[fromId=SAV2001, toId=CUR3001, amount=Money[amount=50000, currency=INR]]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Domain-Driven Design gives me tactical building blocks for modeling inside a single service and strategic concepts for organizing across services. On the tactical side, an Entity has a unique identity and a changing lifecycle, so at National Bank of India an Account is an entity identified by its account number, and two accounts with the same balance are still different because their ids differ. A Value Object has no identity, is immutable, and is compared by value, so I model Money as a Java record holding an amount and a currency, which kills the whole class of bugs where someone passed a raw BigDecimal and accidentally mixed rupees with dollars.

An Aggregate is a cluster of entities and value objects treated as one consistency unit and accessed only through its Aggregate Root, so all changes go through account.debit and account.credit, which enforce the never-negative invariant. A Repository abstracts persistence for one aggregate root, mapping in Spring to an interface extending JpaRepository, with exactly one repository per aggregate root. A Domain Service holds stateless business logic that spans entities and belongs to no single one, like a transfer rule across two accounts. An Application Service orchestrates the whole use case, manages the transaction, and calls domain services and repositories, mapping to the Spring @Service annotated with @Transactional, and crucially it contains no business rules itself.

On the strategic side, a Bounded Context is the boundary within which one model and one Ubiquitous Language are consistent, where the team uses the same exact words in code, docs, and conversation. Context Mapping describes how contexts relate, through a shared kernel, a customer-supplier relationship, or an anti-corruption layer that translates another context's model at the border. Domain Events are records of something meaningful that happened, published to decouple contexts, so my Deposits context emits a FundsTransferred event and the Lending and Notification contexts react without sharing the Deposits model.

The way I summarize it in an interview is that the tactical blocks keep one service's model clean and expressive, while the strategic concepts stop many services from collapsing back into a tangled shared model. When I apply both together, each service speaks its own precise language, protects its own invariants through aggregate roots, and communicates with the rest of the bank through explicit contracts and domain events rather than reaching into each other's data.
